en.title: Chris Hansen Blasts A24's 'Primetime' as an "Insult," Defends 'Predator' Legacy
en.summary: Former 'To Catch a Predator' host Chris Hansen has labeled A24's upcoming film 'Primetime' an "insult," expressing strong disapproval of the fictionalized portrayal of his controversial career. Hansen stands by his past sting operations, even those that ended in tragedy, and refused to sign an NDA before walking out of a screening.
en.body:
The sting operations of **Chris Hansen**'s groundbreaking series, *To Catch a Predator*, remain a pivotal, albeit often debated, chapter in television history. Now, A24's upcoming film, **Primetime**, which fictionalizes Hansen's career and stars **Robert Pattinson** as the host, has drawn sharp criticism from Hansen himself. He has unequivocally called the film an "insult," signaling a deep dissatisfaction with how his work and its consequences are being depicted.

Directed by **Lance Oppenheim**, *Primetime* is based on **Luke Dittrich**'s 2007 Esquire article, "Tonight on Dateline, This Man Will Die." The article chronicled the tragic suicide of a Texas prosecutor who was targeted in one of the show's sting operations. Hansen, speaking to The Hollywood Reporter, made it clear he has no regrets about the methods employed on *To Catch a Predator*, even in the face of such devastating outcomes. He emphasized the industry's broader issues, stating, “We’re talking about an industry that was led by perhaps one of the biggest predators to walk the planet, Harvey Weinstein.” His stance suggests a belief that the film misrepresents or trivializes the gravity of the situations his show addressed.

## A Host's Fierce Defense

Hansen's opposition to *Primetime* is so profound that he walked out of a screening after being asked to sign a non-disclosure agreement, which he refused. This act underscores his firm stance on the narrative presented in the film. He views the portrayal as potentially harmful, especially given the sensitive nature of the cases featured on *To Catch a Predator*. The show, while lauded by some for its direct approach to confronting online predators, was also criticized for its confrontational style and the intense emotional toll it took on all involved. Hansen's current position suggests he feels *Primetime* fails to capture the nuances or the intended purpose of his investigative work, potentially miscasting him as a villain or misinterpreting the show's impact.

## The Community's Unease

The controversy surrounding *Primetime* resonates deeply with audiences who followed *To Catch a Predator* closely. For many, Hansen's show was a stark, albeit uncomfortable, look at a dark side of the internet that was still emerging. The film's release raises questions about accountability, the ethics of true crime dramatizations, and the lasting impact of media on real-life events and individuals. Fans are particularly interested in how A24 will navigate the sensitive subject matter and whether the film will offer a balanced perspective or lean into a more sensationalized narrative. The potential for the film to be perceived as an "insult" by its subject matter highlights the fine line between compelling storytelling and disrespectful exploitation.

## What's Next

*Primetime* is set to premiere at the Venice Film Festival on September 5th. It remains to be seen how the film will be received by critics and audiences, especially given **Chris Hansen**'s vocal disapproval and the sensitive nature of its source material. Further details regarding a wider release are expected to be announced following the festival.
